Essential revisions:

1) The authors need to more carefully interpret protein levels in their experiments. Throughout the text, the authors conclude that the levels of Hsp104, ɑ-synuclein, and TDP-43 do not change enough to affect their preferred interpretations. However, levels of the Hsp104 variants vary over at least an order of magnitude (Figure 1D, Figure 2C, Figure 3B, Figure 5C). The authors need to consider Hsp104 variant levels when arguing that one Hsp104 variant is more effective than another (e.g. subsection “Diverse Hsp104 homologs selectively suppress TDP-43 toxicity and aggregation in yeast”).

Furthermore, some Hsp104 variants reduce expression of toxic proteins (i.e., A503S in Figure 1D, Figure 2D, Figure 3B). The text needs to properly acknowledge that alterations in toxic protein expression could be a mechanism by which some Hsp104 variants suppress toxicity (e.g. subsection “Hsp104 homologs prevent TDP-43 aggregation in human cells”, sentence beginning with, "We also monitored mClover3-TDP-43∆NLS…").

2) Some experiments lack important controls. In Figure 4, the authors should also analyze worms lacking both ɑ-synuclein and Hsp104 as well as worms expressing the Hsp104 variants alone. This control will help the reader to understand: (a) whether the loss of DA neurons is ɑ-synuclein-specific, and (b) whether the Hsp104-dependent rescue of DA neurons is ɑ-synuclein-specific. In Figure 5G,H, the authors should include un-aggregated luciferase controls so the reader can better understand the magnitude of luciferase refolding induced by these Hsp104 variants.

3) The result that these Hsp104 variants could suppress toxicity by a disaggregase-independent mechanism is a compelling finding that requires an additional control. Because many of these Hsp104 variants have not been biochemically characterized before this work, the authors should demonstrate that the canonical walker A, pore loop, and walker B mutations used in Figure 6 disrupt disaggregase activity in the expected manner. The authors could use the same luciferase assay from Figure 5G,5H with wild-type, walker A mutant, pore loop mutant, and walker B mutant variants of S. cerevisiae Hsp104 as well as Hsp104 from one of the more exotic species.

4) Subsection "Hsp104 homologs prevent TDP-43 aggregation in human cells":

a) Regarding the observation that ScHsp104WT also reduced the proportion of HEK293T cells with TDP-43 aggregation at 24-hours post transfection while it did not in yeast cells (Figure 3C vs. Figure 1G), the authors did not address if this is just a protein artefact in utilizing mClover3-TDP-43ΔNLS instead of TDP-43-GFP, or if it reflects differences in cellular environments or factors related to Hsp104 activity that are unaccounted for. It should be emphasized that the latter possibility requires attention as it raises the problem of relevance in using the yeast model to approximate the human cell, despite the authors' justification by referencing such practice by other groups. It is thus prudent that the authors repeat some of the TDP-43 experiments for ScHsp104WT in yeast cells using mClover3-TDP-43ΔNLS instead of TDP-43-GFP, for example.

b) In tracking the TDP-43 foci formation at 24-hours versus 48-hours post transfection, the authors did not address as to why the magnitude of increase in % cells with foci from 24-hours to 48-hours displayed by no-Hsp104 (vector-only) control is drastically lower compared to all other cells co-expressing a Hsp104 homologue. One explanation is the unaccounted protein overexpression-induced stress / toxicity experienced by cells co-transfected with an Hsp104 homologue that is absent in the vector-only (no Hsp104) control, which will likely make the results more difficult to interpret.

c) Western blots for samples at 48-hours post transfection is missing.

5) Subsection "αSyn-selective Hsp104 homologs prevent dopaminergic neurodegeneration in C. elegans":

a) Regarding the interpretation of lack of neuroprotection by CtHsp104 due to target promiscuity, this argument will be convincing once CtHsp104 is shown to also fail in providing neuroprotection against TDP-43 toxicity compared to Hsp104 homologues that are specific against TDP-43 using the C. elegans model (TDP-43 toxicity in C. elegans model: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20530643). This data is currently missing from the manuscript.

6) Subsection "Differential suppression of proteotoxicity by Hsp104 homologs is not due to changes in disaggregase activity":

a) Regarding the authors' statement on potentiated Hsp104 disaggregases having elevated ATPase and disaggregase activities: Even though this has been shown previously, ScHsp104(A503S) or another potentiated mutant should be included in the biochemistry assays presented as a positive control, which will validate the experimental procedures employed and importantly, to provide conclusive evidence that the natural Hsp104 homologues are indeed "potentiated" differently compared to the artificially potentiated mutants.

b) In Figure 5C, the authors should also include Western blots showing normal induction of Hsp26 or other heat shock-inducible proteins as confirmation that the yeast strains used are not compromised in heat shock response.

c) In Figure 5E, the authors should label the individual rescuer and non-rescuer Hsp104 homologues; the current figure is not very informative.

d) Although the authors presented extensive biochemistry data showing the ATPase and disaggregase activity of Hsp104 homologues, there is no discussion in regard to the oligomerization state, which can be assessed using a variety of experimental techniques, including native PAGE, size exclusion chromatography, analytical ultracentrifugation, negative-stain electron microscopy, etc. In fact, examination of oligomeric state becomes particularly important in the authors' investigation of Hsp104 domains that contribute to suppression of aggregate toxicity, as chimeric proteins or isolated cognate domains may not form the expected hexameric form. Furthermore, data pertaining to the particular oligomeric state of the chimeras / cognate domains are expected to provide valuable information in establishing the molecular / structural basis of any retention of loss of toxicity suppression activity.

7) Subsection "ATPase-independent passive chaperone activity underlies suppression of TDP-43 and αSyn toxicity by Hsp104 homologs":

a) Regarding the authors' claim of Hsp104 homologues in suppressing aggregate toxicity via passive chaperone activity: Although the authors have provided extensive, thorough yeast genetics data showing that neither the ATPase nor substrate translocation activity is required for aggregate toxicity suppression, to claim passive chaperone activity being the molecular basis requires additional experimental proof, such as comparing the refolding rate of thermally denatured reporter proteins (e.g. luciferase) in the presence or absence of Hsp104 homologues, their respective chimeric proteins or isolated cognate domains.

8) In subsection “Diverse Hsp104 homologs selectively suppress TDP-43 toxicity and aggregation in yeast” and subsection “Distinct Hsp104 homologs selectively suppress αSyn toxicity and inclusion formation in yeast”, referring to the data In Figure 1—figure supplement 3: Suppression of TDP-43 or αSyn toxicity by select Hsp104 homologs is a substrate-specific effect (related to Figure 1 and Figure 2). The authors make the claim that "MbHsp104, SrHsp104, CrHsp104, PeHsp104, and GsHsp104, which all suppress TDP-43 toxicity, do not suppress αSyn nor FUS toxicity" (panel A) and that "TtHsp104 and TlHsp104 do not suppress TDP43 nor FUS toxicity" panel B and that "other Hsp104s investigated in this study do not suppress toxicity of TDP-43 (left), αSyn (middle), or FUS (right)" (panel C). While most of the data here support the authors conclusions, the wording "does not suppress" is a very strong statement. The data is not completely convincing. For example, in panel C, for the FUS overexpression (right panel) ChtHsp104 and StHsp140 seem to show some suppression of toxicity. Similarly, MtHsp104, StHsp104 and TaHsp104 for α-Syn maybe show some slight suppression. I don't think this changes the nature of the conclusion; however, the authors should be a little more cautious in their choice of wording and/or better discuss the data if they feel that there is compelling evidence that absolutely no suppression is shown.

9) In subsection “Diverse Hsp104 homologs selectively suppress TDP-43 toxicity and aggregation in yeast”: the authors state "Hsp104 homologs were consistently expressed,.… (Figure 1D)". The data on the Western Blot for Hsp104 (anti-flag in the blot in Figure 1D) is not convincing. The levels of protein look variable. Perhaps a quantification of replicates could be added to show whether Hsp104::flag protein levels are indeed consistent? Similarly, in Figure 2 panel C the Western blot could also be more convincing with replication and quantification. In Figure 5C, the Western Blot and the text that refer to it show variation in the levels of expression as well. For example, ScHsp104, TtHsp104 and GsHsp104 show much higher protein levels than StHsp104, MtHsp104 and ChtHsp104 yet the text claims: "These differences are not due to differences in expression, as all homologs were consistently expressed, as confirmed by Western blot (Figure 5C)". ScHsp104, TtHsp104 and GsHsp104 are among the highest rescue of thermotolerance. Contrast this with Figure 7—figure supplement 1, where the expression levels look much more consistent, with only CtHsp104 ∆N from the HSP104 promoter (panel F) showing lowered expression. The chimeras presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 also show some variation in levels. In summary, the differences in expression levels for these experiments should be better quantified if possible and should be discussed in more depth regarding possible effects on the data, especially given the reliance on ectopic expression throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Prokaryotic ClpGGI, but not ClpB or hyperactive ClpB variants, suppresses TDP-43, FUS, and α-synuclein toxicity in yeast. ClpGGI potently suppresses αSyn toxicity and slightly suppresses TDP-43 and FUS toxicity, while ClpB and hyperactive variants (ClpBK476D and ClpBY503D) are ineffective against all three substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C56-C58, and C60-C63 collectively demonstrate through yeast spotting assays and Western blots that ClpGGI has therapeutic properties while ClpB variants do not. The data show consistent expression levels and no effect on substrate protein levels, supporting that the differences are due to specific disaggregase properties rather than expression artifacts.

results.result: Five eukaryotic Hsp104 homologs (Mb, Sr, Cr, Gs, Pe) selectively suppress TDP-43 toxicity and foci formation in yeast without restoring nuclear localization. These homologs suppress TDP-43 toxicity as effectively as the potentiated variant A503S but through a different mechanism that does not require restoration of nuclear TDP-43 localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C31-C43 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 1C), Western blots (Figure 1D-F), and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1G-I) showing that these homologs suppress TDP-43 toxicity and foci formation without significantly affecting TDP-43 expression levels or inducing a heat shock response. The data demonstrate that toxicity suppression can occur independently of nuclear relocalization.

results.result: Two eukaryotic Hsp104 homologs (Tt and Tl) selectively suppress α-synuclein toxicity and restore αSyn plasma membrane localization in yeast. These homologs are substrate-specific, showing minimal effect on TDP-43 or FUS toxicity, and suppress αSyn foci formation by restoring membrane localization in ~75% of cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C44-C51 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 2B), Western blots (Figure 2C-E), and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2F-G) demonstrating selective suppression of αSyn toxicity without affecting expression levels or inducing HSR. The data show clear restoration of membrane localization correlated with loss of cytoplasmic foci.

results.result: Natural Hsp104 homolog PeHsp104 and engineered variant A503S show enduring reduction of TDP-43 aggregation in human HEK293T cells. At 48 hours post-transfection, PeHsp104 and A503S maintain significantly lower proportions of cells with TDP-43 aggregates compared to wild-type ScHsp104, which shows only transient suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C65-C73 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3E) and Western blots (Figure 3B-D) showing that PeHsp104 and A503S maintain TDP-43 aggregate suppression at both 24 and 48 hours, while ScHsp104 and SrHsp104 show only day 1 effects. The suppression occurs without reducing TDP-43 expression levels, indicating a direct effect on aggregation.

results.result: TtHsp104 and TlHsp104 protect dopaminergic neurons from α-synuclein-mediated neurodegeneration in C. elegans. Coexpression of these homologs results in ~40% of worms maintaining normal DA neurons at 7 days post-hatching, comparable to potentiated Hsp104 variants, without intrinsic toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C76-C79 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4A-B) confirming expression, DA neuron scoring (Figure 4C), and microscopy (Figure 4D) showing significant neuroprotection. Controls demonstrate the homologs are not intrinsically toxic (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and the level of protection is comparable to previously validated potentiated variants.

results.result: CtHsp104 fails to suppress α-synuclein toxicity in C. elegans DA neurons and TDP-43 aggregation in HEK293T cells despite suppressing both in yeast. This suggests that promiscuous activity in yeast does not necessarily translate to effectiveness in metazoan systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by C. elegans DA neuron survival data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and HEK293T flow cytometry data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) showing no significant protection or aggregate reduction. This contrasts with CtHsp104's effectiveness in yeast (Figures 1B, 2A), suggesting substrate-specific homologs may be more effective in complex systems.

results.result: Specific Hsp104 homologs (Mb and Cr) inhibit TDP-43 aggregation in vitro through an ATP-independent mechanism. These homologs inhibit TDP-43 aggregation in the presence or absence of ATP, whereas ScHsp104 has limited efficacy, suggesting a passive aggregation-inhibition mechanism distinct from active disaggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by in vitro TDP-43 aggregation assays (Figure 6D-E) showing that MbHsp104 and CrHsp104 inhibit aggregation both with and without ATP, while ScHsp104 is less effective. Control experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) confirm the effect is not due to inhibition of TEV protease cleavage. Thermotolerance and luciferase disaggregation data (Figures 5-6) support that differences are not due to general disaggregase activity.

results.result: The majority of therapeutic Hsp104 homologs (Gs, Mb, Sr, Ct, Tt, Tl) suppress TDP-43 or α-synuclein toxicity through an ATPase-independent mechanism that does not require canonical substrate translocation. Mutations in Walker A, Walker B, and pore-loop motifs that abolish disaggregase activity do not affect toxicity suppression by these homologs, contrasting with the potentiated variant A503S which requires these motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C88-C100 are supported by extensive mutagenesis data (Figure 7) showing that mutations abolishing ATPase activity and substrate translocation do not impair toxicity suppression by most homologs. Western blots confirm mutant expression and thermotolerance assays confirm loss of disaggregase function. The contrast with A503S (Figure 7B) demonstrates a fundamentally different mechanism of action for natural homologs.

results.result: The NTD is required for toxicity suppression by specific Hsp104 homologs (Mb, Cr, Tt) but not others (Gs, Pe, Sr, Ct, Tl). NTD deletion abolishes TDP-43 toxicity suppression by MbHsp104 and CrHsp104, and α-synuclein toxicity suppression by TtHsp104, indicating the NTD plays a substrate-specific role in some but not all homologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 7D-E, I) showing that ΔN mutants of Mb, Cr, and Tt lose toxicity suppression activity while ΔN mutants of other homologs retain activity (Figure 7C, F-H, J). This demonstrates heterogeneity in the structural requirements for toxicity suppression among different homologs.

results.result: The NTD, NBD1, and MD regions of TDP-43-selective homologs contain sequence determinants crucial for passive inhibition of TDP-43 aggregation. Chimeras with NTD:NBD1:MD from TDP-43-selective homologs fused to ScHsp104 NBD2:CTD phenocopy TDP-43 suppression but not α-synuclein suppression, and disruption of cognate domain interactions abolishes activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by chimera spotting assays (Figure 8B-F) showing that cognate NTD:NBD1:MD units are necessary and sufficient for TDP-43 toxicity suppression when combined with ScHsp104 NBD2:CTD. The substrate specificity is maintained (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and disrupted chimeras lose activity, demonstrating the importance of coordinated domain interactions.

results.result: Proteotoxicity suppression is an emergent property of hexameric Hsp104 homologs and cannot be recapitulated by monomeric fragments. Fragments of PeHsp104 and SrHsp104 encompassing NTD:NBD1:MD or NBD2:CTD do not reduce TDP-43 toxicity, indicating that hexamerization is required for function.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 8G) showing that Hsp104 fragments fail to suppress TDP-43 toxicity despite containing domains identified as important for activity. This is consistent with the known requirement for hexamerization in Hsp104 function and suggests that the passive aggregation-inhibition mechanism also requires the hexameric architecture.

results.result: The NBD2:CTD unit of α-synuclein-selective homologs (Tt and Tl) is necessary but not sufficient for suppression of α-synuclein toxicity. Chimeras with either NTD:NBD1:MD or NBD2:CTD from Tt/Tl fail to suppress αSyn toxicity, indicating that both regions contribute to substrate specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by chimera spotting assays (Figure 9B-E) showing that neither NTD:NBD1:MD nor NBD2:CTD from Tt or Tl alone is sufficient to confer αSyn toxicity suppression. This contrasts with TDP-43-selective homologs and suggests a more complex structural requirement for αSyn specificity.

results.result: Chimeras with non-cognate NTD:NBD1 units fused to ScHsp104 MD:NBD2:CTD can gain α-synuclein suppression activity, mimicking potentiated variants. A chimera with CtHsp104 NTD:NBD1 fused to ScHsp104 MD:NBD2:CTD suppresses αSyn toxicity more strongly than CtHsp104WT, and a similar PeHsp104 chimera gains αSyn activity despite PeHsp104 being TDP-43-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 9F, Figure 8—figure supplement 2D) showing unexpected gain of αSyn suppression activity in specific chimeras. The toxicity of these chimeras at 37°C (Figure 8—figure supplement 3, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) and comparison to known potentiated variants support the interpretation that disrupting NTD:NBD1:MD interactions can mimic potentiation.

results.result: All Hsp104 homologs except PfHsp104 are non-toxic to yeast at 30°C and 37°C. PfHsp104 is more toxic than the potentiated variant A503V at 37°C, consistent with its repurposed role as a membrane-embedded translocon component rather than a soluble disaggregase.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C124 are supported by spotting assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing growth defects only for PfHsp104. The lack of toxicity for other homologs contrasts with some potentiated variants and is consistent with natural selection filtering out deleterious sequences. The PfHsp104 toxicity is explained by its different biological function (C30, supported by citations).

results.result: Hsp104 homologs that suppress the same substrate (TDP-43 or α-synuclein) show higher sequence identity to each other than to homologs with different substrate specificities. TDP-43-suppressing homologs have mean pairwise identity of 56%, αSyn-suppressing homologs 76%, while cross-group comparisons average 44%.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by sequence identity calculations (Supplementary file 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) showing quantitative differences in sequence similarity that correlate with substrate specificity. However, the biological significance is limited as no clear sequence motifs were identified (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2), and phylogenetic clustering is imperfect (Figure 1A).

results.result: Natural eukaryotic Hsp104 homologs display substrate specificity, typically suppressing either TDP-43 or α-synuclein toxicity but not both (except CtHsp104), and no homologs were found that suppress FUS toxicity. This contrasts with potentiated variants which typically suppress multiple substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by comprehensive screening data (Figures 1-2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing selective toxicity suppression patterns. The contrast with potentiated variants is supported by citations (C123) and data showing A503S suppresses multiple substrates (Figure 7B). This represents a key distinction between natural and engineered variants.

results.result: Natural eukaryotic Hsp104 homologs act through ATP-independent passive inhibition of aggregation rather than enhanced disaggregase activity. These homologs suppress toxicity without requiring disaggregase activity, instead utilizing genetic variation outside core AAA+ features for substrate-specific molecular recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131, C135-C136 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: mutagenesis showing ATPase-independence (Figure 7), in vitro aggregation assays showing ATP-independent inhibition (Figure 6D-E), similar disaggregase activities despite different toxicity profiles (Figure 6B-C), and thermotolerance data showing no correlation with toxicity suppression (Figure 5). This represents a major mechanistic finding distinguishing natural from engineered variants.

results.result: Background on Hsp104 function and neurodegenerative disease: Hsp104 is a protein disaggregase that reverses stress-induced aggregation and can disassemble disease-associated protein aggregates including α-synuclein, polyglutamine, and others. Potentiated variants have been engineered but can show off-target toxicity, while natural variation remains largely unexplored.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C27 provide established background knowledge supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims establish the rationale for the study by describing known Hsp104 functions, disease contexts, therapeutic potential, and limitations of current approaches. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature and provide appropriate context.

results.result: Discussion and speculation: Natural Hsp104 homologs have likely been filtered by natural selection to avoid deleterious sequences, while engineered variants are potentiated by destabilizing the NBD1:MD interface. The authors speculate that enhanced disaggregase activity may come at the cost of substrate specificity and propose future development of modular disaggregases combining potentiating mutations with molecular-recognition motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128, C137-C138 represent speculation and proposed future directions rather than experimental findings. While C125-C127 are reasonable inferences from the data showing natural homologs lack toxicity while engineered variants can be toxic, C128, C137-C138 are explicitly speculative proposals for future work. These claims provide valuable discussion but are not directly supported by experimental evidence in the manuscript.

results.result: Prior knowledge about Hsp104's dual role: Hsp104 functions both as a molecular chaperone preventing aggregation and as a disaggregase reversing aggregation, with both activities requiring ATPase activity for maximum effect, though disaggregase activity is more sensitive to reduced ATPase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 are supported by citations to prior literature (Shorter and Lindquist, 2004; 2006) and provide important context for interpreting the current findings. This background establishes that while both activities typically require ATP, they have different sensitivities, which is relevant for understanding the ATP-independent mechanism discovered in this study.
